title: You’ll Need Rules
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart draws on Eisenhower's decision before D-Day, as told in Lead Yourself First, to argue that professionals manage complexity by simplifying, withdrawing into solitude, and writing until they reach a single guiding rule. He applies the idea to his own life, citing rules such as leaving work at 5 pm and publishing on set days, and claims that rule-lessness gives only the illusion of freedom, borrowing Jim Collins's genius of the AND. He then turns to the classroom, defending teacher-set rules like raising hands against the evaluation-rubric orthodoxy that rules should be co-created with students. For him the final authority is the teacher's own professional expertise and a guiding aim of long-term flourishing through mastery without sacrificing one's soul. The conclusion is that both teachers and classrooms will need rules. A course promotion appears at the end.
points: Eisenhower's example shows a repeatable process for hard decisions: simplify, get alone, write until a single rule emerges.
Personal rules about work hours and publishing days create freedom by removing needless complexity, which Stuart frames as freedom AND restraint.
Stuart contends that teacher-imposed classroom rules are legitimate even when evaluation rubrics reward co-created ones, because expertise outranks the rubric.
His proposed guiding rule for educators is to promote students' long-term flourishing through mastery, but not at the expense of the teacher's soul.
quotes: First, he sought to simplify. He aimed to reduce the complexity, as Stephen Ambrose writes in Supreme Commander, “into its essentials, extract a principal point, and then make that point his guiding star for all decisions.

But second (and more importantly for our purposes today), Eisenhower got all by himself and wrote about the situation until he had boiled it down to a single, guiding rule. “We must go unless there is a real and very serious deterioration in the weather,” he decided.

It’s this activity set — withdrawing to solitude, writing for clarity, and arriving at a rule through which to govern behavior when once again we return to the pressure of work — that I write to impress upon us today. This is the work that we need to become better at this coming school year, perhaps more than any other.

To live a life without rules creates only the illusion of freedom. Were I to allow myself to write only when I felt the pull, or work at any hour for the sake of my students, then I am certain I would be a less free man today than I am, not a freer one.
So it’s not just popular to disdain inflexible rules imposed from without — it’s dogma, enshrined in the very rubrics of our guild.
The evaluation rubric can’t be the final authority for the professional teacher; instead, one must follow a guiding rule derived from the hulk of one’s ever-growing professional expertise.

For you and me, I think that guiding rule is something like, “We must promote the long-term flourishing of young people by means of helping them master as much as possible this year, albeit none of this at the expense of our souls.
